passage:
"Reena, want to play the flower game?"
"Again, Amma?"
"Again. Smell the rose." Sudha held up an imaginary flower.
Reena sniffed hard, belly puffing out.
"Now blow out the birthday candle. Slowly, slowly."
Reena blew till her cheeks were empty. "Can I do bubbles next?"
"Bubbles. Big, slow ones, or they pop."
They played it every evening, when nothing was wrong.
On Friday, Reena's block tower crashed. She stamped, face crumpling. Then she stopped, sniffed an invisible rose, and blew out a long, wobbly candle.

qa.q: What did Reena blow out after smelling the rose?
qa.a: Reena blew out the birthday candle.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when her tower crashed?
qa.a: Reena was frustrated and upset; she stamped and her face crumpled.

qa.q: Why did Sudha practise the game when nothing was wrong?
qa.a: Practising while calm made the slow breathing easy for Reena to reach when upset, as it was on Friday.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel watching Reena sniff the invisible rose on Friday?
qa.a: Sudha would likely feel proud and relieved to see the game working on its own.

grounding: A young child learns slow breathing through a flower, candle and bubble game practised when calm, then reaches for it when upset.

passage:
Teacher's note, Sunflower Group. Ira Kapoor.
This month we practised "bubble breathing" at calm circle times: breathe in, then blow one long, slow bubble through a wand. Tejas loved it.
Today thunder crashed during snack time. Tejas dropped his banana, clapped his hands over his ears and began to wail. I knelt by him and asked, "Can you blow me a big bubble?" He took a shaky breath and blew out long and slow, no wand needed. Then another. His hands came off his ears. I'll tell his father at pickup.

qa.q: What did Tejas drop when the thunder crashed?
qa.a: Tejas dropped his banana.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when he clapped his hands over his ears?
qa.a: Tejas was frightened by the thunder and began to wail.

qa.q: Why did Ira's question "Can you blow me a big bubble?" work?
qa.a: Tejas had practised bubble breathing while calm, so the familiar game was easy to reach when he was scared.

qa.q: What would change if the class had only tried bubble breathing for the first time during the storm?
qa.a: Tejas would probably not know the game well enough to use it while frightened, so it would help far less.

grounding: A young child learns slow breathing through a bubble game practised when calm, then reaches for it when frightened.

passage: On a quiet evening on the rooftop of their house in Bundi, Seema made up a game for Gautam. 'Smell the jasmine,' she said, holding a flower under his nose. He sniffed long and slow. 'Now blow out the diya, gently.' He puffed, and the flame wobbled. They did it again and again, giggling. Every night that week they played. On Sunday at the fair, Gautam lost his balloon and started to howl. Seema knelt. 'Where's your jasmine?' Gautam sniffed his fingers, then blew. Smell, blow. His howls slowed to sniffles.

qa.q: What did Seema hold under Gautam's nose?
qa.a: A jasmine flower.

qa.q: How was Gautam feeling when he lost his balloon at the fair?
qa.a: He was very upset and howling over the lost balloon.

qa.q: Why did practising every night help at the fair?
qa.a: Because Gautam had learned the game while calm, the slow breathing was easy to reach when he was upset.

qa.q: How might Seema feel when Gautam used the game at the fair?
qa.a: She probably felt pleased and proud that their rooftop game was working.

grounding: Shows a young child learning slow breathing through a flower-and-candle game practised when calm, and using it when upset.

passage: Every bath time in their Osaka flat, Hana gave Ivan a bubble wand. 'Slow, slow, big bubble,' she said. If he blew too hard, the bubble popped. If he blew long and gentle, a huge one floated up to the ceiling. Ivan loved it. After a week he could make bubbles the size of his head. Then came the doctor's visit for his check-up. When the doctor reached for the stethoscope, Ivan started crying. Hana bent down. 'Big bubble?' Ivan sniffed and blew a long, slow, pretend bubble. Then another. His crying faded, and he let the doctor listen.

qa.q: What did Hana give Ivan at bath time?
qa.a: A bubble wand.

qa.q: What was Ivan feeling when the doctor reached for the stethoscope?
qa.a: He was scared and started crying.

qa.q: Why was it wise to practise bubble breathing at bath time?
qa.a: Learning it while calm and having fun made it easy for Ivan to use when he was frightened.

qa.q: How might the doctor have seen Ivan's pretend bubbles?
qa.a: The doctor probably appreciated how Ivan calmed himself, making the check-up easier for everyone.

grounding: Shows a young child learning slow breathing through a bubble game practised when calm, which he can use when upset at the doctor's.

passage: In the kindergarten circle in Margao, Maria Teacher held up a paper flower and a paper candle. 'First we smell the flower, slow and long. Then we blow out the candle, soft and slow.' The children sniffed and blew, laughing. They did it every morning before prayers. On Thursday, Nitin tripped in the playground and grazed his hand. He screamed, then sat crying hard. Maria Teacher crouched. 'Nitin, can you find your flower?' Nitin sniffed, shakily. 'Now the candle.' He blew. Three times. His crying slowed enough for her to wash the graze.

qa.q: When did the children practise the flower and candle?
qa.a: Every morning before prayers.

qa.q: How was Nitin feeling after he tripped?
qa.a: He was hurt and upset, screaming and crying hard.

qa.q: What made the breathing work for Nitin in the playground?
qa.a: He had practised it every morning when calm, so he could find it when upset.

qa.q: How might the other children see the flower and candle game?
qa.a: They probably saw it as a fun morning game, without knowing it was giving them a tool for hard moments.

grounding: Shows young children learning slow breathing through a flower-and-candle game practised when calm, which a child uses when upset.

passage: I'm Nilesh, Bhavna's big brother, and I watched Mumma teach her a game. Every evening when Bhavna was calm, they played 'smell the flower, blow the candle'. Bhavna sniffed a pretend flower slowly, then puffed at a pretend candle. Sometimes they blew bubbles through a straw, as slowly as possible. I thought it was silly. Then at the fair, Bhavna lost her balloon and started crying hard. I don't know what she was thinking, but she sniffed, blew one slow puff, then another. Mumma did it with her. After a few puffs her crying slowed down.

qa.q: What game did Mumma and Bhavna play?
qa.a: 'Smell the flower, blow the candle'.

qa.q: What might Bhavna have been feeling when she lost her balloon?
qa.a: She was upset and sad, crying hard at losing the balloon.

qa.q: Why did practising when calm help at the fair?
qa.a: The slow-breathing game was already familiar, so Bhavna could reach for it when she got upset.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see the game after the fair?
qa.a: Nilesh probably no longer thinks it's silly, having seen it help his sister calm down.

grounding: A young child learns slow breathing as a game when calm and can reach for it when upset.
